prize_parts.citation: for the optical detection and coherent control of single electron spins of nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond at room temperature

statement.case_for: B001 is the clearest case on the shortlist of a new tool that opens a door. The optical detection of a single NV centre (Wrachtrup group, 1997) and the coherent control of its electron and nuclear spins at room temperature (Jelezko and Wrachtrup, 2004) are original experiments that anyone can reproduce and verify, and they have been reproduced in very many laboratories for over two decades. The downstream reach is real: nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and strain sensing, NMR on small numbers of molecules, sensing inside cells, and spin qubits used in network experiments. It is a discovery and an invention at once, which is what the Physics Prize is for, and it is mature enough that there is no doubt about the result. Two names keep the credit tied to the original experiments rather than to the later, more elegant extensions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Single-spin detection and coherent control were followed within a few years by work from other groups (Delft, Harvard, Stuttgart, Chicago), and the committee may judge that the field's identity is now quantum sensing, where Lukin's role is larger than in the original experiments. A two-name prize would then look narrow. A further concern is that the downstream benefit to humanity is still more promised than delivered in some areas, particularly biology. Compared with B031 or B029, this candidate has the least support among colleagues in the opening round, and I must not mistake my own first-place ranking for evidence that others share it.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B001 sixth and proposed Wrachtrup, Jelezko and Lukin, noting that credit is divisible between single-spin detection, coherent control and later sensing and network work, and that Hanson and Awschalom are not credited. He ranked B031 first as a theory prediction followed by a decisive experiment.
responses.response: I agree that the division of credit is the central difficulty, and I do not dismiss Hanson or Awschalom. But I would resist adding Lukin only to cover the later sensing and quantum-register developments, because those were built on the original detection and control experiments and the mandate asks for the original work. I would accept Lukin only if the committee frames the citation around quantum sensing as a field, and I would then want the historical record checked on who first demonstrated each sensing capability. On B031 I share your enthusiasm for a clean new material platform, and I rank it second, but I would apply the same test to the experimental credit: Cao, the lead student, is not on our list, and the committee should say openly how it handles that.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B029 first, valuing optical lattice clocks at 10^-18 as a measurement advance with exceptional clarity of metric, and ranked B001 fifth, asking whether the sensing impact has reached prize-defining level and noting the Wrachtrup overlap with another ballot.
responses.response: I take the clarity of the clock metric seriously, and as an experimentalist I value it. My reservations are about novelty and benefit. Hall and Hänsch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already covered the comb and ion-clock territory, and I ranked B029 last of my eight because the societal impact is still largely prospective until the second is redefined. On your question about NV sensing, I would point to the broad adoption already visible, in condensed-matter, materials and chemistry laboratories and in commercial instruments, which is a concrete record rather than a promise. I do accept that B029 is the stronger candidate on the strict criterion of experimental maturity and on the number of independent laboratories reaching comparable performance, and that is why I name it as an alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B031 first, arguing that the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gave a transparent mechanism for flat bands and that the 2018 experiments confirmed it, creating a whole field of moiré quantum matter. He also ranked B029 second.
responses.response: I agree that this is a rare case in which a simple prediction was followed by a striking experiment, and I see the force of the argument. My difference is about timing and attribution. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and the sample-to-sample variability from twist-angle disorder makes me want longer experience before the committee fixes the credit. I also think the 'three-person' version needs more care than the opening ballots gave it: if Bistritzer is credited as a postdoc co-author of the theory, the committee must be ready to explain why Cao and the other early experimentalists are not. I would not block B031, but I would not make it my first choice yet.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B013 first, arguing that the BeppoSAX afterglow localisation plus optical and radio follow-up settled the cosmological origin of gamma-ray bursts, and ranked B012 third on the grounds that the experimental side of the Higgs discovery has never been honoured.
responses.response: B013 is a real discovery from nature, and the combination of a wide-field X-ray camera with rapid follow-up is exactly the kind of instrument-enabled result that I admire. My concern, which you also raise, is that the credited three do not cover the optical identification and redshift work, and that Jan van Paradijs, whose role was central, cannot be honoured. I would want to be absolutely sure who did the original localisation and who did the original optical detection before I could support it. On B012, I agree the detectors are extraordinary, but I am cautious about a prize for the leaders of collaborations of thousands when the physics was recognised in 2013; the Committee would need a very clear statement of what the three individuals specifically conceived and built.

uncertainties: Exact priority and division of credit between single-centre optical detection (1997) and coherent control (2004), and the roles of Gruber and co-authors, which I am recalling from memory and should be checked against the record.
Whether the committee prefers a quantum-sensing framing that would bring Lukin in, or a narrower citation for the original optical-detection and control experiments with two names.
Whether B031 is mature enough given the unsettled pairing mechanism, and how the committee would handle Cao and the early experimental credit.
Whether B029 is sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes to count as a new discovery.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have no known collaboration with Wrachtrup, Jelezko, Lukin or the other credited names. As an electron microscopist at Chalmers I share an institution with Göran Johansson, who is close to the superconducting-circuit community in B004, but that does not affect B001.
